# Linked zero inflation

This vignette provides code for fitting the linked zero-inflated model of @smith2012 in brms [@burkner2017] and Stan, in place of the OpenBUGS code published with the original papers.
In the linked model, the probability of an excess zero, $\pi$, is a logistic function of the log of the mean of the count distribution, $\lambda$:
$$
\text{logit}(\pi_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \log(\lambda_i),
$$
where $i$ indexes observations and $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ are parameters to be estimated.
Smith et al. [-@smith2012; -@smith2014] supplied R and OpenBUGS [@lunn2009] code for fitting this model, but OpenBUGS has now largely been superseded by more modern software.
In brms, the model requires only the zero-inflated negative binomial family that brms provides and a non-linear formula [@burkner2018], with no custom family or Stan code, and the functions for prediction and model checking (`posterior_epred()`, `posterior_predict()`, `loo()`, and `pp_check()`) work on the fitted model without modification.

Here is how to implement the linked model in brms, with `y` a count and `x1`, `x2`, and `group` standing for the predictors in any particular study:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(brms)

fit <- brm(
  formula = bf(
    y ~ eta,
    nlf(zi ~ g0 + g1 * eta),
    eta ~ x1 + x2 + (1 | group),
    g0 ~ 1,
    g1 ~ 1,
    nl = TRUE
  ),
  data   = my_data,
  family = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior  = c(
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "eta"),
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "g0"),
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "g1")
  )
)
```
:::


The linear predictor for $\log(\lambda)$ is declared as a non-linear parameter, `eta`, which then enters both the formula for the mean and the formula for `zi`, the brms name for $\pi$.
The zero-inflated negative binomial family in brms has a log link for the mean and a logit link for `zi`, so each formula is written on the scale of its linear predictor, and `zi ~ g0 + g1 * eta` is the linked model of @smith2012.
The two parameters of the link, `g0` and `g1`, are non-linear parameters, each with an intercept only.
A non-linear model in brms requires a proper prior on every non-linear parameter, so the coefficients of `eta`, `g0`, and `g1` each need one.
Because $\gamma_1$ multiplies $\log(\lambda)$, rescaling the counts shifts $\log(\lambda)$ by a constant, which changes $\gamma_0$ but not $\gamma_1$, so a prior for $\gamma_1$ does not depend on the units of the counts.

# Snapper in and around Te Whanganui-A-Hei (Hahei) Marine Reserve

The example uses counts of legal-sized snapper, *Chrysophrys auratus* (Sparidae), formerly *Pagrus auratus*, from baited underwater video deployments in and around Te Whanganui-A-Hei (Hahei) Marine Reserve, New Zealand, analysed by @smith2012 and, with two other reserves, by @smith2014.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(brms)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybayes)

snapper <- read_csv(
  "data/snapper-hahei.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    reserve = factor(reserve, levels = c("outside", "inside")),
    season  = factor(season, levels = c("spring", "autumn")),
    area    = factor(area),
    year    = factor(year)
  )
```
:::



::: {.cell}

:::


Each of the 348 counts is the maximum number of legal-sized snapper seen in any one frame of a video (MaxN), from 6 areas (3 inside the reserve), 9 years, and two seasons.
Zeros made up 55% of the counts: 83% of those outside the reserve, where the mean count was 0.32, and 28% of those inside, where the mean count was 3.39.

Following @smith2012, the model for $\log(\lambda)$ included reserve status and season as fixed effects, and area and year as random effects.
We used Normal(0, 2.5) priors for the coefficients of `eta`, `g0`, and `g1`, which are weakly informative on the log scale of $\lambda$ and the logit scale of $\pi$, a half-Student-t prior with 3 degrees of freedom and scale 2.5 for the standard deviations of the random effects, and Gamma(0.01, 0.01), the brms default, for the shape parameter of the negative binomial.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
f_linked <- bf(
  count ~ eta,
  nlf(zi ~ g0 + g1 * eta),
  eta ~ reserve + season + (1 | area) + (1 | year),
  g0 ~ 1,
  g1 ~ 1,
  nl = TRUE
)

pr_linked <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "eta"),
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "g0"),
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "g1"),
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 2.5), class = "sd", nlpar = "eta"),
  prior(gamma(0.01, 0.01), class = "shape")
)

fit_linked <- brm(
  formula = f_linked,
  data    = snapper,
  family  = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior   = pr_linked,
  chains  = 4,
  iter    = 3000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  seed    = 2012,
  file    = "fits/fit-linked"
)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

:::


Four chains of 2,000 post-warmup draws each were run with `adapt_delta = 0.99`.
The largest $\hat{R}$ was 1.002, and none of the 8,000 post-warmup transitions were divergent.

The number of zeros in data simulated from the fitted model can be compared with the number observed:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
zeros_linked <- snapper |>
  add_predicted_draws(fit_linked) |>
  group_by(.draw) |>
  summarise(zeros = sum(.prediction == 0))
```
:::


The posterior predictive distribution of the number of zeros had a median of 190 (95% interval 170 to 211), against 191 observed.

The function `add_epred_draws()` in [tidybayes](https://mjskay.github.io/tidybayes/) calls `posterior_epred()`, which returns the predicted mean count, $(1 - \pi)\lambda$, with $\pi$ computed through the link.
With `dpar = TRUE`, it also returns $\lambda$ (`mu`) and $\pi$ (`zi`).
Here it was evaluated for every sampled combination of area, year, and season:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pred_draws <- snapper |>
  distinct(area, reserve, year, season) |>
  add_epred_draws(fit_linked, dpar = TRUE) |>
  ungroup()
```
:::


The predicted mean count for each area and season, averaged over the years in which that combination was sampled, is shown with the observed counts in @fig-data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the figure"}
# Average the predicted mean counts over years within each area and season,
# then summarise the draws.
pred_area_season <- pred_draws |>
  group_by(area, season, .draw) |>
  summarise(
    mean_count = mean(.epred),
    .groups    = "drop_last"
  ) |>
  median_qi(mean_count)

season_cols <- c(
  spring = "#009E73",
  autumn = "#D55E00"
)

# The areas inside the reserve (2 to 4) are shaded.
set.seed(1)
ggplot() +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 1.5,
    xmax = 4.5,
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#FFF5C2"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = snapper,
    aes(
      x      = area,
      y      = sqrt(count),
      colour = season
    ),
    position = position_jitterdodge(
      jitter.width  = 0.2,
      jitter.height = 0.15,
      dodge.width   = 0.7
    ),
    alpha = 0.4,
    size  = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = pred_area_season,
    aes(
      x     = area,
      y     = sqrt(mean_count),
      ymin  = sqrt(.lower),
      ymax  = sqrt(.upper),
      fill  = season,
      group = season
    ),
    position  = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
    shape     = 21,
    colour    = "black",
    size      = 0.6,
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = sqrt(c(0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 30)),
    labels = c(0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 30)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  labs(
    x      = "Area",
    y      = "Legal-sized snapper per deployment (MaxN)",
    colour = "Season",
    fill   = "Season"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Comparison with negative binomial and constant zero-inflation models

To check whether the link improved the model, we fitted two alternatives with the same predictors for $\lambda$ and the same priors: a negative binomial model with no zero inflation, and a zero-inflated negative binomial model with constant $\pi$.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pr_glm <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "b"),
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 2.5), class = "sd"),
  prior(gamma(0.01, 0.01), class = "shape")
)

fit_nb <- brm(
  formula = count ~ reserve + season + (1 | area) + (1 | year),
  data    = snapper,
  family  = negbinomial(),
  prior   = pr_glm,
  chains  = 4,
  iter    = 3000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  seed    = 1,
  file    = "fits/fit-nb"
)

fit_constant <- brm(
  formula = bf(
    count ~ reserve + season + (1 | area) + (1 | year),
    zi ~ 1
  ),
  data    = snapper,
  family  = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior   = c(
    pr_glm,
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "zi")
  ),
  chains  = 4,
  iter    = 3000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  seed    = 2,
  file    = "fits/fit-constant"
)
```
:::



::: {.cell cache.extra='["16af73efa8e91decfdf8d51827d4752a","de673fe7df7aa792ce80b2c0dcca4a24","cc53d80d1c84dc69f75fbbd01d7a665f"]'}

```{.r .cell-code}
loo_linked   <- loo(fit_linked, reloo = TRUE)
loo_constant <- loo(fit_constant, reloo = TRUE)
loo_nb       <- loo(fit_nb, reloo = TRUE)

loo_compare(loo_linked, loo_constant, loo_nb)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
        model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff diag_elpd
   fit_linked       0.0     0.0      NA                    
 fit_constant      -6.4     4.2    0.93                    
       fit_nb      -7.2     4.5    0.94                    
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

:::


Expected log predictive density, estimated by Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation [PSIS-LOO, @vehtari2017], was greatest for the linked model, exceeding that of the model with constant $\pi$ by 6.4 (SE 4.2) and that of the negative binomial model by 7.2 (SE 4.5).
Each difference was less than twice its standard error, so the support for the link from these data is moderate.
Observations with a Pareto $k$ value above 0.7, the threshold above which PSIS-LOO estimates are unreliable [@vehtari2017], were handled by refitting the model without them (`reloo = TRUE`).

The model with constant $\pi$ estimated a probability of an excess zero of 0.11 (0.01 to 0.22).
The median number of zeros predicted was 183 for the model with constant $\pi$ and 180 for the negative binomial model, against 191 observed and 190 for the linked model.
A constant $\pi$ applies equally to deployments inside and outside the reserve, whereas the proportion of zeros was 83% outside and 28% inside.

# Estimated relationship between zero inflation and the mean count


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_linked |>
  gather_draws(b_g0_Intercept, b_g1_Intercept) |>
  median_qi()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 7
  .variable      .value .lower .upper .width .point .interval
  <chr>           <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>  <chr>    
1 b_g0_Intercept  0.313 -0.921  1.54    0.95 median qi       
2 b_g1_Intercept -1.52  -2.51  -0.764   0.95 median qi       
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

:::


The probability of an excess zero decreased as the mean count increased, with a posterior median for $\gamma_1$ of −1.52 (95% credible interval −2.51 to −0.76), and for $\gamma_0$ of 0.31 (−0.92 to 1.54) (@fig-link).
Averaged over the 72 sampled combinations of area, year, and season, the probability of an excess zero was 0.68 (0.49 to 0.79) outside the reserve and 0.19 (0.09 to 0.27) inside.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the figure"}
# The relationship for every posterior draw, over a grid of lambda.
curves <- link_draws |>
  expand_grid(lambda = exp(seq(log(0.1), log(20), length.out = 100))) |>
  mutate(pi = plogis(b_g0_Intercept + b_g1_Intercept * log(lambda)))

median_curve <- curves |>
  group_by(lambda) |>
  summarise(pi = median(pi))

set.seed(2012)
curves_100 <- curves |>
  filter(.draw %in% sample(unique(.draw), 100))

# Posterior medians of lambda and pi for each sampled combination.
cell_points <- pred_draws |>
  group_by(area, reserve, year, season) |>
  summarise(
    lambda  = median(mu),
    pi      = median(zi),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = curves_100,
    aes(
      x     = lambda,
      y     = pi,
      group = .draw
    ),
    colour    = "grey60",
    alpha     = 0.3,
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = median_curve,
    aes(
      x = lambda,
      y = pi
    ),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = cell_points,
    aes(
      x      = lambda,
      y      = pi,
      colour = reserve
    ),
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      outside = "#D55E00",
      inside  = "#0072B2"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x      = expression("Mean of the negative binomial component (" * lambda * ")"),
    y      = expression("Probability of an excess zero (" * pi * ")"),
    colour = "Reserve status"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The black line is the posterior median of $\pi$ at each value of $\lambda$, and the grey lines are the relationship for 100 draws from the posterior distribution of $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$. Each point marks the posterior medians of $\lambda$ and $\pi$ for one sampled combination of area, year, and season, coloured by reserve status. # Reserve effect

The reserve effect is the ratio of the mean count inside the reserve to the mean count outside it, computed within each posterior draw from the predicted mean counts in `pred_draws`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
reserve_effect <- pred_draws |>
  group_by(.draw, reserve) |>
  summarise(
    mean_count = mean(.epred),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = reserve,
    values_from = mean_count
  ) |>
  mutate(ratio = inside / outside)

reserve_effect |>
  median_qi(ratio)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  ratio .lower .upper .width .point .interval
  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>  <chr>    
1  11.1   7.46   16.7   0.95 median qi       
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

:::


Averaged over the 72 sampled combinations of area, year, and season, with equal weight for each, mean counts were 11.1 (7.5 to 16.7) times greater inside the reserve than outside.
This ratio applies to the areas and years that were sampled, and does not include the variation expected among new areas or years.
The ratio is smaller than the 16.4 reported by @smith2012, which evaluated $(1 - \pi)\lambda$ at zero area, year, and season effects instead of averaging it over them.

# Other implementations

@anderson2022 fitted the zero-inflated negative binomial with the link of @smith2012, which they called ZINBL, by maximum likelihood in the R package [senlm](https://primer-e.github.io/senlm/), with a non-linear function for the mean response of a species along a single environmental gradient.
@rabel2023 fitted a Bayesian version in Stan, also along a single gradient, in the R package [modskurt](https://hdrab127.github.io/modskurt/) ([source on GitHub](https://github.com/hdrab127/modskurt)), with $\pi$ linked to the mean count divided by the peak mean count along the gradient, rather than to the log of the mean count.
